t: The core of the book is the Zhou yi, a divination manual of the Western Zhou, which modern scholars date to between the 10th and 4th centuries BCE.
Over the Warring States and early imperial periods it gained the Ten Wings and became a cosmological text; in 136 BCE Emperor Wu of Han named it the first among the classics.
Commentators of many schools have read it for divination, moral guidance and philosophy, and it has been translated into Western languages dozens of times.
dyk: The Zuo Zhuan and Guoyu describe more than twenty divinations with the Zhou yi, made by professional soothsayers for royal families between 671 and 487 BCE, yet none of the stories uses a commentary or a stated method.
ev: last quarter of the 9th century BCE
Edward Shaughnessy dates the compilation of the Zhou yi in its current form to the early reign of King Xuan of Zhou
The Zuo Zhuan and Guoyu record more than twenty divinations using the Zhou yi for royal families
The Great Commentary, arguably the most important of the Ten Wings, is composed, and a Shanghai Museum copy shows the Zhou yi in use at all levels of society
Emperor Wu of Han names the Zhou yi the first among the classics and calls it the I Ching
Wang Bi writes his Annotated Book of Changes, which becomes the official commentary under the Tang
Zhu Xi reconstructs yarrow stalk divination from the Great Commentary, a method still in use
Leibniz writes the first European commentary on the I Ching
Richard Wilhelm's German translation appears; Cary Baynes's English version follows in 1950

f.made: A divination manual of the Western Zhou, traditionally ascribed to Fuxi, King Wen of Zhou, the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, an attribution no longer generally accepted; the Ten Wings commentaries are later and of unknown origin
f.form: A text in Early Old Chinese of 64 hexagrams, each with a name, a hexagram statement and six line statements (two extra for hexagrams 1 and 2), bound with ten commentaries called the Ten Wings
f.where: The oldest known manuscript, found in 1987, is held by the Shanghai Library; other early copies come from the Shanghai Museum's bamboo slips (found in 1994) and from Mawangdui (found in 1973); the official edition was cut in stone as one of the Xiping Stone Classics
f.known: 64 hexagrams and 8 trigrams; the King Wen sequence; yarrow stalk and coin divination; the Ten Wings; one of the Five Classics; Leibniz's binary reading; Richard Wilhelm's 1923 German translation
